procedural_history.impugned_order: Judgment and Order dated June 1, 1970 of the Allahabad High Court in Criminal Appeal No. 1931 of 1969 and Referred No. 182 of 1969.
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: The Sessions Judge convicted Samman Dass of murder and sentenced him to death. The Allahabad High Court, on appeal and in a reference for confirmation of the death sentence, set aside the conviction and acquitted him.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The State of Uttar Pradesh appealed to the Supreme Court by special leave, challenging the High Court's judgment. The Supreme Court accepted the appeal, set aside the judgment of the High Court and convicted the accused-respondent under section 302 I.P.C.

directions: Set aside the judgment of the High Court

issue.issue_text: Whether the Supreme Court, in an appeal under Article 136 of the Constitution, is justified in interfering with a High Court's judgment that reverses a trial court's conviction, especially when the High Court's grounds are found to be manifestly fallacious and untenable.

law.fact_text: This Court in an appeal under article 136 of the Constitution A does not normally re-appraise the evidence and interfere with the assessment of that evidence by the High Court.
law.law_text: The general rule is that the Supreme Court, in an appeal under Article 136, does not normally interfere with the High Court's assessment of evidence.

law.law_text: An exception to the general rule exists: the Supreme Court will interfere if the High Court has caused a grave injustice by acting on grounds that are plainly untenable.

application.application_text: The intervention is specifically justified when the High Court reverses a trial court's judgment on grounds that are found to be "manifestly fallacious and untenable" or "wholly untenable."

reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court decided that while it does not normally interfere with a High Court's assessment of evidence, it is justified in doing so when the High Court reverses a trial court's conviction on grounds that are manifestly fallacious, untenable, and result in a grave injustice. The High Court's duty to independently assess evidence does not shield its decision from Supreme Court review if its reasoning is fundamentally flawed.

application.fact_text: The Supreme Court established that while it does not normally interfere with the High Court's assessment of evidence, it is not prevented from doing so.

application.fact_text: The Court's power to interfere is triggered when the High Court reverses a trial court's judgment on grounds that are "manifestly fallacious and untenable" or "plainly untenable," resulting in a grave injustice.
application.label: reasoning

application.fact_text: The Court explicitly stated that the High Court's specific duty under Section 374 of the Code of Criminal Procedure to independently appraise evidence does not shield its decision from Supreme Court review if the reversal is based on such flawed grounds.
application.label: reasoning

application.fact_text: In the specific case, the Court found that the High Court had indeed reversed the conviction on grounds that were "wholly untenable," thus justifying the Supreme Court's intervention.

reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court decided that its power to correct a grave injustice allows it to interfere with a High Court's order, even one made under its duty to independently appraise evidence per Section 374. This interference is justified if the High Court's reasons for reversing a trial court's judgment are found to be manifestly fallacious and untenable.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the Supreme Court, in an appeal under Article 136 of the Constitution, is justified in interfering with a High Court's judgment that reverses a trial court's conviction, especially when the High Court's grounds are found to be manifestly fallacious and untenable.
appellant_arguments: The Supreme Court should interfere with the High Court's decision because a grave injustice has been done.
The High Court's interference with the trial court's decision was based on grounds that are plainly untenable and its view is clearly unreasonable on the evidence.
Interference is warranted if the High Court acts perversely or otherwise improperly.
respondent_arguments: The Supreme Court should not readily interfere with the findings of fact given by the High Court.

arguments.issue_text: Does the High Court's duty to independently appraise evidence for itself in a reference under Section 374 of the Code of Criminal Procedure prevent the Supreme Court from interfering with its order if the grounds for reversing the trial court's judgment are manifestly fallacious and untenable?
appellant_arguments: The Supreme Court's power to interfere is not prevented by the High Court's duty, especially when the High Court's grounds for reversal are wholly untenable and it has acted perversely or improperly.
respondent_arguments: The Supreme Court should not interfere with the findings of fact given by the High Court, as the High Court has a duty to appraise the evidence for itself.

cases.case_name: Himachal Pradesh Administration v. Shri Om Prakash
cases.citation: Cr. Appeal No. 61 of 1969 decided on December 1, 1971
cases.principle: The fact that the High Court, in a reference under s. 374 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, has to appraise the evidence for itself and has to arrive at its own independent conclusion would not prevent the Supreme Court from interfering with the order of the High Court if the High Court reverses the judgment of the trial court on grounds which are manifestly fallacious and untenable.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: Under Article 136 of the Constitution, the Supreme Court will interfere with a High Court's assessment of evidence if the High Court reverses the judgment of a trial court on grounds which are manifestly fallacious, untenable, and clearly unreasonable, resulting in a grave injustice.
obiter: In criminal matters, no distinction can be made as a matter of construction between a judgment of conviction and one of acquittal.

legal_tests_applied: The Supreme Court will interfere with a High Court's assessment of evidence if it finds that a grave injustice has been done by the High Court interfering with the trial court's decision on grounds which are plainly untenable.
The Supreme Court will interfere if the view taken by the High Court is clearly unreasonable on the evidence on record.
Interference is called for if the High Court acts perversely or otherwise improperly.
The Supreme Court can interfere if the High Court reverses a trial court judgment on grounds which are manifestly fallacious and untenable.
